newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel chief appeals to UN over refugees.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel chief appeals to UN over refugees.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Sunday his forces captured the strategic town of Lubutu and appealed to the United Nations to help some 170,000 refugees trapped in the fighting.

Kabila said his forces overran the makeshift Tingi Tingi refugee camp on Saturday, dislodging Rwandan and Burundian refugees who had fled fighting further east. There has been no independent confirmation of the claim.

"Many hundreds of refugees are coming and our men have been ordered not to harm them ... the United Nations is invited to go to Tingi Tingi to help the refugees to return home and help repatriate them," Kabila told a news conference in the eastern city of Goma.
Kabila suggested aid agencies would be able to fly into Tingi Tingi immediately to encourage the refugees to return.

Aid workers who were evacuated on Saturday from Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city, reported seeing tens of thousands of refugees at Tingi Tingi, 200 km (125 miles) southeast, preparing to flee the rebel advance on Friday.
Doctors said up to 40 refugees a day were dying of hunger and disease.
The Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (ADFL) controls most of eastern Zaire after launching a war in October to topple Mobutu Sese Seko, President of Zaire since 1965.

Kabila said his troops captured Tingi Tingi and the strategically-important town of Lubutu nearby and its airstrip after heavy fighting on Saturday afternoon in which one rebel and 25 Zairean soldiers were killed.
Lubutu, 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Kisangani, is the last town on the road from Bukavu and boasts an airstrip.
The rebel advance towards Kisangani threatens the integrity of the vast and mineral-rich country.

Kabila said any ceasefire was ruled out before negotiations, adding he refused to sign an agreement to end the fighting on a visit to South Africa last week -- despite foreign diplomatic pressure to do so.
"The Alliance waits for an invitation saying that Mobutu has written to the organisers to say that he personally will negotiate. Only then will we negotiate," Kabila said.
South African President Nelson Mandela met Kabila and an aide to Mobutu last week in an attempt to broker peace.
Mobutu, now in France ailing with prostate cancer, has decided to delay his return home for a few days to pursue his search for a solution to the crisis, an aide said on Sunday.
The delay is unrelated to Mobutu's health, the aide added. His entourage earlier said he would return home at the weekend.

The Tingi Tingi refugees are said to include members of the Interahamwe militia and former Rwandan government army held responsible for the 1994 Rwanda genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, appealed on Saturday to both sides in the conflict to spare refugees and grant access to aid agencies.
A Zaire defence ministry statement read on state radio criticised the decision by aid agencies to pull out of Kisangani, arguing it violated their mandate.

The rebels, who have captured a swath of territory in east Zaire around 1,000 km (625 miles) long, responded to a January 20 counter-offensive by attacking on several fronts, throwing the notoriously ill-disciplined Zaire army on the defensive.
The rebels said they took Kindu, 400 km (250 miles) south of Kisangani, on Friday, a claim confirmed by independent sources but denied by the Zaire government.
Kabila said he had advanced to 50 km (35 miles) beyond Kindu after fierce fighting on Saturday, capturing a large quantity of armaments in the process.
The rebels have identified Kisangani as a target. The city is a gateway to east Zaire and the last navigable point on the Zaire River that flows southwest to Kinshasa.
